data.title: RICTOR regulates an interspecies crosstalk that influences longevity through a methionine cycle-mitophagy axis
data.authors: Motwani S; Bhandari S; Chitkara S; Ujjainiya R; Ghosh P; Sengupta S; Mukhopadhyay A

evidence.label: Animal model
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.model_system: Caenorhabditis elegans: rict-1 (RICTOR, mTORC2) mutants on E. coli OP50 versus vitamin B12-rich Comamonas diets; metr-1 and mmcm-1 dependence; mitochondrial morphology, mitophagy, osmotic-stress and lifespan assays
data.finding: In the worm C. elegans, loss of the mTORC2 component RICTOR (rict-1) extended lifespan and raised osmotic-stress tolerance only on vitamin B12-rich bacterial diets with optimal methionine. The benefit required two B12-dependent enzymes, METR-1 (methionine cycle) and MMCM-1 (propionate breakdown), and a rise in succinate that fragments mitochondria and switches on mitophagy, which the authors found indispensable for the longevity. Evidence is from one invertebrate species and genetic loss of function; it does not show that mTORC2 inhibition extends lifespan in mammals or humans.
data.abstract_excerpt: Adaptive modulation of physiological traits in response to dietary fluctuations is essential for organismal fitness and is governed by complex gene-diet interactions that remain mechanistically unexplored. Here, we identify the conserved mTORC2 component RICTOR as a critical regulator of dietary plasticity in Caenorhabditis elegans. Loss of rict-1/RICTOR confers enhanced osmotic stress tolerance and longevity on vitamin B12-rich bacterial diets containing optimal methionine.

extracted_findings.intervention: rict-1 (RICTOR) loss of function; vitamin B12-rich bacterial diet
extracted_findings.effect: Loss of rict-1 extends lifespan and osmotic-stress tolerance on B12-rich diets; requires METR-1, MMCM-1, succinate-driven mitochondrial fragmentation and mitophagy
